pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 10–11: solve multi-step problems in context, DECIDING which of the four operations and methods to use at each step and WHY. The skill is strategic (planning and justifying), not just executing arithmetic.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y6): 'solve problems involving addition, subtraction, multiplication and division' and 'solve problems involving […] the four operations', deciding which operations and methods to use and why.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): builds on 4.OA.3 (multistep word problems with the four operations, interpreting remainders, assessing reasonableness) and the Grade 5–6 progression; Standards for Mathematical Practice MP1 (make sense of problems) and MP4 (model).
• Operational details — the child reads a rich context, identifies knowns/unknowns, PLANS a sequence of steps, chooses an operation per step with a reason, executes (using secured written methods incl. long division and remainder interpretation), then CHECKS reasonableness with estimation/inverse. Bar/part-whole models are the bridge from words to operation choice.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): solve a two-to-three-step problem mixing operations with support in laying out steps. Tier B (10–11): solve a three-step four-operation problem independently and JUSTIFY each operation choice. Tier C (11): find and correct a wrong-operation error in a given multi-step solution, explaining the fix.
bestPractices: Teach a problem-solving routine (understand → represent → plan → do → check) rather than answer-hunting; the deliberate representation and planning steps are where operation choice is decided.

Use bar models / part-whole diagrams to expose STRUCTURE — a comparison bar signals subtraction or division, equal groups signal multiplication or division — so operation choice follows from the model, not from keyword-spotting.
Explicitly kill keyword strategies ('altogether = add', 'left = subtract'): give problems where the keyword misleads, forcing the child to reason from the situation's structure.

Make justification routine — 'why this operation here?' after every step — and use error-analysis tasks (a worked solution with a wrong-operation step) so children articulate WHY an operation is right or wrong.
Always close with a reasonableness check via estimation or inverse operations, connecting to the estimation topic (mt_ilPrU0cbtT) so checking becomes automatic and catches wrong-operation slips.
keyRepresentations: Bar model / part-whole diagram translating the situation into visible structure (comparison bars, equal-group bars) from which the operation follows.
A step-planner / flow layout: box per step showing the operation chosen, the reason, and the intermediate result feeding the next step.
Worked-and-flawed solution pairs for error analysis — one correct, one with a wrong-operation step — placed side by side.
Number-sentence chain with a letter for the final unknown, linking each step's result to the next (connects to representing with equations).
commonMisconceptions: Keyword-matching instead of modelling the situation ('share' → always divide even when it means 'each gets, so total = ×').
Losing the thread across steps — using the wrong intermediate value or forgetting a step in a three-step chain.
Choosing an operation by which numbers are 'easy' to combine rather than by the situation's structure.
Skipping the reasonableness check, so a wrong-operation answer (often wildly off) goes unnoticed.
Mishandling the remainder at a step (rounding up vs down vs keeping) because the context isn't re-examined.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11, develop strategic multi-step problem solving: deciding WHICH of the four operations each step needs, in what ORDER, and WHY. The skill is planning, justifying and monitoring a solution — not just executing arithmetic. Learners move words → structural model (bar/part-whole) → operation choice → execution → reasonableness check, can record the plan as a number-sentence chain (a letter for the final unknown, with each step's result feeding the next), and also analyse flawed solutions to spot a wrong-operation step.

activities.title: Problem planner: build the model, then choose the operation
feedback: If the chosen operation mismatches the structure, the model visibly fails to resolve (comparison bars don't line up, or equal groups don't fill the total) — a cue to re-read what the situation is asking, not to try another keyword.
A structurally correct choice resolves the model and produces an intermediate value; carry that value into the next step rather than re-reading raw numbers.
For the worked answer: 6×24 = 144 pencils; 144÷8 = 18 per class; 18−5 = 13 left per class. Check each step with the inverse and against your estimate.
If the exact answer is far from your estimate, suspect a wrong operation or a carried-forward error and re-examine the step.
activities.rationale: Operation choice is a planning skill, so making the words→model→operation chain the interactive core (with the model visibly matching or mismatching the situation) puts reasoning, not arithmetic, at the centre. Writing the plan as a number-sentence chain with a letter for the final unknown links each step's result to the next and connects to representing situations with equations. Dragging quantities into bars, live resolution/failure of the model, and the intermediate value auto-feeding the next step are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve problems involving all four operations, deciding which operations and methods to use and why, including multi-step problems in context.
Bar-model / part-whole representations help pupils choose operations from problem structure rather than keyword-matching.

Pupils solve multistep word problems with the four operations, represent them with equations using a letter for the unknown, and assess the reasonableness of answers using estimation including rounding.
learnerActions: Read a rich context, e.g. 'A school buys 6 boxes of 24 pencils. They share them equally between 8 classes. Then each class uses 5 pencils on the first day. How many are left in each class?'
Before computing, represent the situation as a bar / part-whole model: drag the quantities into comparison bars or equal-group bars so the structure is visible.
For step one, choose the operation and state a reason tied to the structure (e.g. 'multiply, because there are 6 equal groups of 24').
Carry the intermediate result forward into the next step's model, then choose the operation for that step, and repeat to the final answer.

Record the plan as a number-sentence chain in which each step's result feeds the next and the final unknown is a letter — for example 6×24 = p; p÷8 = c; c−5 = n, where n is the final unknown you are solving for — so the connection between steps is explicit.
Before revealing the exact answer, estimate it and state whether the exact result is reasonable.
activities.intendedInsight: The situation's STRUCTURE — not a keyword — dictates which operation each step needs, and a multi-step problem is one connected chain where each result feeds the next.

activities.title: Spot and fix the wrong-operation step
feedback: If the learner cannot find the error, prompt: 'What question is this step actually answering? Does the operation match?'
Confirm the fix by checking the corrected final answer against a rough estimate and the inverse of each step.
activities.rationale: Error-analysis with a worked-and-flawed solution pair makes justification and self-monitoring explicit, targeting the common habit of keyword-matching and the failure to check reasonableness.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve problems involving all four operations, deciding which operations and methods to use and why, including multi-step problems in context.
learnerActions: Examine a completed multi-step solution placed beside the problem, where one step used the wrong operation (e.g. subtracted where it should have divided).
Locate the flawed step and explain why that operation does not match the situation's structure.
Correct the step, re-run the remaining chain with the fixed intermediate value, and confirm with an estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify why an operation is right also means being able to detect why one is wrong — monitoring a solution is part of solving it.

activities.title: Socratic planning dialogue
feedback: When the learner picks an operation by which numbers are 'easy' to combine, redirect to the situation: 'What is this step asking for?'
When a step's meaning is unclear, ask the learner to name the unit of the intermediate result (e.g. 'pencils per class').
Note that a phrase like 'in total' here calls for multiplication (6 groups of 24), not addition — a reminder that structure, not a keyword, sets the operation.
activities.rationale: A questioning tutor elicits and probes the plan and the reason behind each choice, mirroring coaching that develops operation-choice. This is one route and emphasises justification over hands-on modelling; it pairs well with the model-building activity rather than replacing it.
sourceClaims: Y6 pupils solve problems involving all four operations, deciding which operations and methods to use and why, including multi-step problems in context.
learnerActions: Work through a word problem with a questioner who never supplies the answer.
Answer probes at each step: 'Why that operation here?', 'What does the number you just found actually represent?', 'Is that reasonable?'
State a plan as a sequence of questions ('first, how many pencils in total across the boxes? then…') and solve one question at a time, writing each intermediate answer.
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising the reason for each operation and what each intermediate value means builds the metacognitive control that multi-step problem solving requires.

activities.title: Annotated exemplar as reference
feedback: Use the exemplar as a model of explanation, then attempt a new problem independently — the reference shows the form of a justified plan, but recognising a good example does not by itself elicit the learner's own planning, so the learner must do the planning themselves.
activities.rationale: A static annotated worked example with tap-to-reveal reasoning is a useful reference, but it does not have the learner choose operations or plan, so it supports rather than substitutes for construction work. It is a scaffold toward independent planning.
learnerActions: Study an exemplar multi-step solution and, step by step, reveal the operation chosen, the reason, and the check for that step.
Compare the exemplar's reasoning to your own plan on a fresh problem.
activities.intendedInsight: A clearly reasoned worked example shows what a complete justified plan and reasonableness check look like.

constraints: Do not teach keyword strategies ('altogether = add', 'left = subtract', 'share = divide'); deliberately include problems where a keyword misleads — e.g. 'share' can mean each gets a portion so the total is found by multiplying — so learners must reason from structure, not the word.

Always close with a reasonableness check: estimate and compare the answer with the context to help catch wrong-operation slips, which are often far off, though not always (e.g. 2+2 and 2×2 give the same answer). Use inverse operations to check each calculation, but remember that an inverse check confirms the arithmetic, not whether the chosen operation was right.

When a step is division, re-examine the context for remainder interpretation (round up, round down, or keep) rather than defaulting to 'r2'; the right handling depends on what the leftover means in the situation.

Multiple-choice/sequencing formats (e.g. 'which operation and why' with reason-distractors such as 'divide because sharing' vs 'multiply because each', ordering the plan, identifying the flawed step) can check strategy during teaching, but they present choices rather than having the learner construct the plan; use them to probe reasoning, not as the sole experience of planning.
The annotated exemplar is a reference scaffold: it shows a justified solution but does not elicit the learner's own operation choices or plan.
If a step produces an arithmetic slip but the operation sequence is correct, treat it as a calculation error (estimate and check with the inverse), not as a planning failure needing reteaching.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
Worked arithmetic checked: 6×24=144, 144÷8=18, 18−5=13 — consistent across the activity, assessment, and source row.

Reinstated the source's 'number-sentence chain with a letter for the final unknown' representation in Activity 1 (which the earlier candidate had dropped despite citing the CCSS-M claim), and clarified that intermediate letters link the chain while the final unknown is the letter being solved for.

Reinstated the concrete reason-distractor example ('divide because sharing' vs 'multiply because each') and the 'share → always divide even when each gets means ×' misconception nuance that had been generalised away.

The claim that choosing a wrong operation makes a bar model 'visibly break' is a design intention for an interactive surface, not an established empirical effect; retained as an optional feedback example, not a guaranteed outcome.
Original source row marks the CCSS-M (4.OA.3) and NCETM claims as verified:false; the only verified:true claim is the DfE Year 6 statement. Evidence strength was not upgraded here.

The row frames 3D as adding 'nothing'; this catalog-fit judgement was not propagated as a universal law. No spatial/3D activity is proposed because the objective is strategic and non-spatial, but no claim is made that 3D could not support any related work.

probeDeeper: Why did you multiply first and not divide first?
What does the 18 you found in the middle actually represent?
In this worked solution someone divided where they should have subtracted — can you find the step and fix it?
Estimate the final answer roughly before checking — is your exact answer sensible?
assess.correctAnswer: 6×24 = 144 pencils; 144÷8 = 18 per class; 18−5 = 13 left per class. The teacher watches for a correct sequence of operation choices (multiply, then divide, then subtract), a stated reason for each, and — in the error-spotting part — the ability to locate the step where a wrong operation was used and correct it.

errorPatterns.pattern: grabs numbers and applies one operation to all of them, or ignores a step — no plan for the sequence
errorPatterns.nextMove: have the child restate the problem as a sequence of questions ('first, how many pencils altogether? then…') and solve one question at a time, writing the intermediate answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child combines 6, 24, 8, 5 in an unstructured way (e.g. adds them, or stops after one step)

errorPatterns.pattern: chooses operations out of order or does not carry the intermediate result forward — e.g. subtracts 5 before sharing
errorPatterns.nextMove: use a bar model or flow diagram where each step's output feeds the next, making the dependency between steps visible.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: steps are done in the wrong sequence so the intermediate quantity is wrong

errorPatterns.pattern: misinterprets a remainder or unit in context when a step is division
errorPatterns.nextMove: ask 'what does the leftover mean HERE?' — tie remainder interpretation to the specific situation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: in a variant with a remainder, child leaves it as 'r2' or rounds wrongly for the context

errorPatterns.pattern: plans correctly but makes an arithmetic slip in one step
errorPatterns.nextMove: do not reteach planning; have the child estimate the final answer and check each step with the inverse.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: correct operation sequence, one wrong calculation; often caught by their own estimate

responseLevels.gap: combines numbers without a plan, applies one operation throughout, or omits steps; cannot spot a wrong-operation step.
responseLevels.full: plans the full sequence, chooses and justifies each operation, carries intermediate results correctly, interprets any remainder in context, and can locate and fix a wrong-operation step.
responseLevels.partial: chooses the right operations for most steps but muddles the order or does not carry the intermediate result forward; finds an error only with heavy hints.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a three-step word problem mixing operations and watch how they plan and choose each step, e.g.: 'A school buys 6 boxes of 24 pencils. They share them equally between 8 classes. Then each class uses 5 pencils on the first day. How many are left in each class?' Watch which operation they pick at each stage and whether they can say why; then show them a worked solution that used the wrong operation at one step and ask them to find and fix it.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Multi-step competence is not four separate skills but knowing WHICH operation each step needs and in what order. Watching the child sequence operations and justify them, plus the error-spotting task, separates children who can execute operations from those who can plan a solution and monitor it — the actual objective.
